dialogue_stages.tutor_prompt: When calculating triangle area from side lengths using Heron's formula, why must we use semiperimeter s instead of total perimeter P?
dialogue_stages.student_response: Because if we used total perimeter P, the differences P - a, P - b, P - c would be too large and change the dimensions.
dialogue_stages.tutor_feedback: Exactly! Dimensionally, [s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)] represents [Length⁴], whose square root gives [Length²] (Area). Furthermore, in any triangle, a + b > c, which ensures s - c = (a+b-c)/2 > 0. If you used P, you wouldn't capture the triangle inequality correctly.

dialogue_stages.tutor_prompt: A triangular plot has sides 6 m, 8 m, 10 m. Calculate its area using Heron's formula, and verify using the standard right-triangle formula.
dialogue_stages.student_response: s = (6 + 8 + 10)/2 = 12. Differences are 12-6=6, 12-8=4, 12-10=2. Area = √(12 × 6 × 4 × 2) = √(576) = 24 m². By right triangle formula: (1/2) × 6 × 8 = 24 m². Both methods agree!
dialogue_stages.tutor_feedback: Outstanding! Verifying Pythagorean triples against base-height formulas is the gold standard for sanity checks.

dialogue_stages.tutor_prompt: What happens to Heron's formula if the three sides form a degenerate triangle, like a = 3, b = 4, c = 7?
dialogue_stages.student_response: s = (3+4+7)/2 = 7. Then s - c = 7 - 7 = 0. The product becomes zero, so Area = 0! That makes sense because a degenerate triangle is just a flat line segment with zero area.
dialogue_stages.tutor_feedback: Brilliant deduction. The boundary case s = c detects degeneracy with zero enclosed area.
